Severity: dry spells can be bridged but yields cannot be sustained in a meteorological drought [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Practice: fanya juu and soil bunds account for the measured losses [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. The actionable distinctions are therefore siting by rainfall regime, farmer-owned rather than imposed structures, and a maintenance horizon of years. On quality, many of the largest gains are from bundled programmes or lender completion reports (Ethiopia public works, India watershed projects, Mauritania), with value of production and forage biomass used as proxies, while the losses come from an Ethiopian synthesis and a matched study; the drought finding is a secondary citation in a review [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_forage_productivity_mrt14_3, ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The nitrogen finding is a content on farm soils, not a yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Household income and returns from soil and water conservation and water harvesting have been found to rise, to stay flat and to fall. Gains run through higher yields, irrigation and diversification: a quasi-experimental study found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_economic_return_mala24_1]; Brazil's production-cistern programme raised family income by about 4.6%, nearly 11% when the top of the income distribution is excluded, with larger effects on farms of 0 to 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_1, ev_household_income_casag22_2, ev_household_income_casag22_5]; a review of 311 Indian watershed case studies found a modest mean benefit-cost ratio of 2.14 and an internal rate of return of 22 percent [ev_economic_return_josh05_1, ev_economic_return_josh05_2]; Mauritanian dikes returned a financial IRR of 24% [ev_economic_return_mrt14_4]; and programme evaluations report income gains of 54% in Karnataka and 58% on the Loess Plateau over control areas [ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_iegchn07_6]. Losses and shortfalls come from costs exceeding gains: in Burkina Faso the yield increase did not cover the annual costs of single SWC measures [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3]; Ethiopian graded fanya juu and graded soil bunds had negative net present values of −148 and −708 ETB per hectare [ev_economic_return_adim16_4]; the Brazilian cistern programme's benefit-cost ratio over its evaluation window was 0.0858 [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]; and in Niger, families with SWC produced a 70 percent surplus in good rainfall years but a 28 percent deficit in low-rainfall years [ev_food_security_kabo04_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: What separates the sides, where the evidence says it: farm size and income, since the Brazilian income effect was positive on small farms but negative on farms larger than 10 ha [ev_household_income_casag22_5, ev_household_income_casag22_6]; labour costing and the size of the initial investment, since Ethiopian household benefit-cost ratios were 0.42 to 0.78 at market wages and exceeded one only with a shadow wage and a low initial investment [ev_economic_return_schmidt12_6]; where structures are built, since off-farm community works gave no food-security or income effect [ev_food_security_abate21_4, ev_food_security_arega24_1, ev_household_income_abate21_2]; the rainfall year [ev_food_security_kabo04_1]; and how long benefits are counted, since the Brazilian ratio covers a short window against a long-lived asset and counts income only [ev_economic_return_casag22_9]. For a Task Team Leader, the practical points are targeting smallholders, costing household labour honestly and expecting returns to arrive over years. On quality, the largest gains are from bundled programmes with weak attribution: IEG calls the China income estimate not robust and notes the India gains may partly be construction wages, and a Karnataka completion report doubts its own before/after figures [ev_household_income_iegchn07_6, ev_household_income_iegind11_2, ev_household_income_kar20_3]. The losses and nulls come mostly from independent evaluations, though the Ethiopian negative values may omit off-site benefits [ev_economic_return_adim16_4], and a Kenyan bundle showed no effect on per capita income [ev_household_income_mala24_2]. Income, returns and food security are proxies for poverty, and the Malawi food-security finding is qualitative and cited second-hand [ev_food_security_ngur26_1]. A cited Burkina Faso statement adds that higher yields improve household food security especially on farms applying manure or some kind of soil and water conservation on over half their plots; it sits on the gain side but does not separate manure from conservation [ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Physical SWC works under public-works and watershed programmes reduce soil loss and downstream runoff, and sediment-control dams with terraces and vegetation trap sediment in the catchment. A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 58.66% and runoff by 53% on average, with soil and stone bunds reducing soil loss by 55.06% and runoff by 49.2% [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_1, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_1, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_4, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_5]; in Ethiopian catchments, stone bunds, check dams and vegetation regrowth cut sediment yield from 8.5 to 1.9 t per hectare a year [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1, ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Nearly all units are programme or lender reports from Ethiopia, India and China, often perception surveys or before/after comparisons; an Uttarakhand water budget showed surface runoff slightly increasing, the Karnataka runoff comparison is against another SWC programme, and IEG doubts the India runoff measurements. Effects mixing runoff and soil-loss metrics are only components of erosion risk. A catchment-restoration meta-analysis in Ethiopia finds minimal effect of catchment treatment on runoff in drought-prone areas with annual rainfall below 500 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_3]. The Ethiopian catchment results combine structures with grazing control and vegetation regeneration and are cited in a review, so the share due to the works is not isolated [ev_erosion_hazard_meko14_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Sediment-control dams, terraces and vegetation in a Loess Plateau watershed programme capture sediment each year, reducing the load reaching downstream rivers.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Single modelled programme-level estimate from a lender review in China, using sediment retention as a proxy for water quality.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Watershed treatment reduces reliance on outside supply: participating villages in India saw reduced water transportation by tanker compared with nonparticipating villages [ev_water_access_deficit_verm19_1], and an agency review credits consumption and production cisterns in semi-arid Brazil with a significant contribution to wider access to water [ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1]. In India, discharge of springs and streams rose in treated watersheds: a sample study in Himachal Pradesh reports a 40 percent increase in water discharge in spring and stream sources [ev_water_regulation_hp17_1], and the Uttarakhand project achieved an average 21 percent increase in water discharge from perennial water sources in sampled micro-watersheds, against a target of 25 percent [ev_water_regulation_utk22_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The tanker reduction is a reported programme assessment [ev_water_access_deficit_verm19_1], and the Brazilian unit is an agency inference from census figures in an upper-middle-income context [ev_water_access_deficit_castro22_1]. The Indian spring and stream discharge figures come from World Bank completion reports, the lender's own evaluation, measured before and after without untreated comparison sites, for catchment treatment that bundles plantations, trenches, ponds and check dams with water-harvesting structures, so the gain cannot be credited to water harvesting alone [ev_water_regulation_hp17_1, ev_water_regulation_utk22_6]. Groundwater-recharge evidence, with its limits, now sits in the catchment water yield rows, which also answer what upstream capture does to water downstream.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger, planting pits in Uganda and conservation tillage with the Magoye ripper in Zambia judge the technologies to cope well with drought [ev_asset_drought_wocat_1219_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1652_2014_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1587_2013_drought, ev_asset_drought_wocat_1139_2013_drought].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, not measurements, with no observed damage or failure data behind them. These are field-level practices, so the ratings describe how the treated fields fare under drought rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Heavy rain overtops or knocks down small field structures: tied ridges in a Kenyan trial collapsed during heavy rainfall events and had to be rebuilt within the season, staggered earth bunds (tabia) in Morocco store the runoff of rains below 50 mm, but in the biggest storms the excess overtops the bunds and gullies the slope [ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av], and WOCAT compilers rate zaï or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger and ripper tillage in Zambia as not coping well with local rainstorms [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1219_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1652_2014_local_rainstorm, ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1139_2013_local_rainstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Ugandan planting-pit compiler rates coping as good [ev_asset_extreme_rainfall_wocat_1587_2013_local_rainstorm]. The Kenyan observation comes from a single-site trial and records rebuilding rather than a loss figure, the Moroccan statement is from a technique manual, and the remaining units are practitioner ratings without damage records [ev_climate_shock_ndun23_1_av, ev_climate_shock_roos10_1_av].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger and conservation tillage with the Magoye ripper in Zambia not to cope well with general river floods [ev_asset_flood_wocat_1219_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1652_2014_general_river_flood, ev_asset_flood_wocat_1139_2013_general_river_flood].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are three practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets, with no observed loss or failure data. Pits, bunds and ripper tillage are field-level practices, so a not-well rating describes exposure of the treated fields to floodwater rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge zaï or tassa planting pits and contour bunds in Niger and planting pits in Uganda to cope well with local windstorms; no unit describes how wind would damage them [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1219_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1652_2014_local_windstorm, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1587_2013_local_windstorm].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: These are three practitioner judgements from documented technology sheets with no observed damage data. Pits and bunds are field-level practices, so the ratings describe exposure of the treated fields rather than damage to a built structure.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: The proximity of zai pits on crusted, degraded soil raises the chances of seed germination and dispersal, so herbaceous and woody species recolonise formerly bare land in Burkina Faso [ev_biodiversity_outcome_roose93_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_zoug14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_kabo04_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Burkina Faso evidence is descriptive, without an untreated comparison, and partly the same observation cited more than once. The only rating, a WOCAT compiler judgement for the Magoye ripper in Zambia, puts animal diversity unchanged, and that conservation-tillage sheet is a loose fit for an in-situ water-harvesting family [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1139_2013_animal_diversity].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for planting pits and stone lines, zai or tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger and planting pits in Uganda rate soil organic matter increased, and the Magoye ripper compiler in Zambia attributes slight biomass and organic matter gains to less soil disturbance [ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1100_2011_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1219_2014_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1652_2014_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_1587_2013_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1139_2013_biomass_above_ground_C]. In the literature, zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter and trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Soil organic matter is a proxy for sequestration, and the Niger and Uganda ratings carry no compiler comment and are practitioner judgements rather than measurements. The literature is mixed: trenches in Mexico reduced soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso detected no significant change in organic matter even though biomass production rose; the conservation-tillage sheet sits at the edge of this family [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The Chinese figures come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country; the contour-tillage values are for the 5-to-10-year window with the greatest increase, not a pooled estimate [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the Maghreb, mechanised bund systems, built with large machines that scrape a 4 to 10 m strip to raise bunds 1.5 to 2 m high every 30 to 50 m, considerably reduce the water collected in downstream hill reservoirs and cost 10 to 25% of the cultivable area [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]. On the other side, earth and stone bunds in Mauritania were built to facilitate water infiltration and replenish groundwater tables, and surveyed communities expressed satisfaction with the rising levels of water in their wells [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1]; in the Peruvian Andes a few studies have observed catchment-level changes such as increased aquifer recharge, which the source calls plausible but not generalisable [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. The sides are measured in different places: the gains are well levels and recharge around the treated land, the loss is water reaching downstream hill reservoirs below mechanised bunds, and a downstream loss can coexist with the local gain. The source ties the loss to mechanised construction and cites it from earlier work in an expert manual; the Mauritanian gain is a lender-reported community perception for works that also included fencing [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1]; and in the Peruvian Andes trenches had little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics key to explaining their impact [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1]. No finding is quantified.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: No-till with a residue mulch reduced total variable costs by 5% against conventional tillage in a Zimbabwe trial, and mulching reduced weed density and labour costs for weeding in an Ethiopian trial [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Two trials, both small savings in recurrent costs rather than the cost of building anything. The Zimbabwe figure is for mulch bundled with no-till against conventional tillage, and the Ethiopian statement gives no figure [ev_project_cost_mash25h1_5, ev_project_cost_sime15h2_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field pits raise infiltration and water retention so crops suffer less from dry spells: zaï gave 300–400 kg of sorghum per hectare in a low-rainfall year on degraded land where the without-zaï yield was 0, only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger, zaï trials let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils with honourable yields in rainfall-deficit periods, and chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s, ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in conservation agriculture meta-analyses report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks where soil water storage reaches 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. Conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect on maize in a Kenyan season with a failed start, and a cited study reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The strongest results are practitioner-reported contrasts from a single Sahelian report, and the conservation agriculture dry-year findings are secondary citations inside meta-analyses rather than pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. Conservation agriculture meta-analyses find immediate positive yield effects when water stress occurs during crop growth, because mulch improves the soil water balance, and maize yields under conservation agriculture generally above conventional practice in seasons with a precipitation balance below 200 mm, rising as conditions get drier [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; in Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis also report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the contrast was 1520 against 400 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In Zambia, a review of conservation agriculture cites trial findings that higher soil moisture improved yields in poor seasons, showing the potential to reduce the risk of crop failure due to low or poorly distributed rainfall [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]. In on-farm conservation-farming trials in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia the largest yield difference over conventional ploughing came in rainy seasons with low rainfall, when the practice maximises rainfall infiltration so the crop can bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season of very scattered rainfall, maize in hand-hoe conservation-farming basins yielded 3,054 kg per hectare against 1,339 kg under ploughing, which the authors say showcased the water-harvesting benefits of the basins [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather put the first-year maize difference between conservation agriculture and ploughing largely in seasons with below normal rainfall, and in the 1980/81 drought year 241 mm produced some maize grain under conservation agriculture and none under ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated out-yielded tilled rice on hillside fields in three seasons that each had a month-long rainfall deficit [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. A commercial farmer in South Africa reported that his no-till, residue-cover and rotation system completely buffered his farm from mild droughts or dry spells through increased rainfall infiltration [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Kenyan trial's short rains with meteorological droughts, tied ridging gave no advantage (0.52 against 0.53 t per hectare without inputs, 1.17 against 1.27 with manure and fertiliser) because there was little or no rainwater to hold in the basins [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. In Mozambique maize and cowpea failed completely on all treatments in the drought season, in long-term Zimbabwe trials mulched and reduced-tillage maize yielded considerably less than conventional tillage in extreme seasons, conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect on maize in a Kenyan season with a failed start, and a study cited in a meta-analysis reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7, ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The family now rests partly on conservation agriculture meta-analyses and on-farm or trial measurements in Malawi, Kenya, Zimbabwe and Mozambique; the zaï and tassa contrasts are author estimates, the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the Kenyan tied-ridging result is a single-site trial [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. Water harvesting is not irrigation, and the new primaries mark the limit: at the more arid Kenyan sites of Laikipia and Machakos each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, with 0 kg per hectare of maize harvested at Machakos due to meteorological drought, and the conservation-farming treatments did not avert it [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The crop model shows the same limit: in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both conservation agriculture and ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the mulch-based system [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5], and in the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The East African low-rainfall gain is for the best system per site, ripping or pitting usually with fertiliser, so it is bundled with reduced tillage and fertiliser, and the authors read it as a trend from their own figure [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. The Zambia 2001/2 basin contrast is a raw comparison in a single season with no normal-year reference, and most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit, so part of the gap is the input package [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The semi-arid drought-year gains are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting, not measured seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. The Madagascar dry-spell gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation and have no normal-year comparison [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. The South African statement is a single commercial farmer's before-and-after testimony for a residue-cover system with no capture structure [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10]. The Zambia review statement is cited secondhand, gives no magnitude and has no normal-year comparison, and the trial behind it bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. Conservation agriculture meta-analyses find immediate positive yield effects when water stress occurs during crop growth, because mulch improves the soil water balance, and maize yields under conservation agriculture generally above conventional practice in seasons with a precipitation balance below 200 mm, rising as conditions get drier [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; in Malawi's El Niño drought season ground cover raised maize from 247 kg per hectare on control plots to 432 kg per hectare and raised the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_food_security_boil19_1]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis also report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. In Zambia, a review of conservation agriculture cites trial findings that higher soil moisture improved yields in poor seasons, showing the potential to reduce the risk of crop failure due to low or poorly distributed rainfall [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]. Farmers practising basins in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Limpopo reported maize and sorghum yields of >1 tonnes per hectare even in seasons with poor rainfall (<450 mm), against total crop failure under conventional ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields too [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather put the first-year maize difference between conservation agriculture and ploughing largely in seasons with below normal rainfall, and in the 1980/81 drought year 241 mm produced some maize grain under conservation agriculture and none under ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated out-yielded tilled rice on hillside fields in three seasons that each had a month-long rainfall deficit [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. A commercial farmer in South Africa reported that his no-till, residue-cover and rotation system completely buffered his farm from mild droughts or dry spells through increased rainfall infiltration [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm, so it does not address seasonal drought [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In Mozambique maize and cowpea failed completely on conservation agriculture and control plots alike in the drought season, with gains only from year two, and a study cited in a meta-analysis reports conservation agriculture yields 5–20% lower than conventional tillage in wet years [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_2, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The conservation agriculture meta-analyses and the Malawi on-farm survey of ground cover give measured support, while the zaï and tassa yield contrasts are author estimates and the dry-year gains in the older meta-analysis are secondary citations [ev_crop_yield_corb20_8, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. Not every in-field practice helped in that Malawi El Nino season: banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare and lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054 [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5, ev_food_security_boil19_3]. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The crop model shows the same limit: in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both conservation agriculture and ploughing [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the mulch-based system [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5], and in the Zimbabwe panel conservation agriculture had no specific impact in mitigating rainfall-shortfall losses for millet and groundnut [ev_crop_yield_mich19_6]. The farmer-reported basin yields compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author warns makes those datasets too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The Zimbabwe panel's drought-season gains are interaction estimates for conservation agriculture as practised (planting basins bundled with residue mulch and rotation); its normal-season results are reported in the production row, not here [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. The semi-arid drought-year gains are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting, not measured seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_1, ev_crop_yield_faocr11_3]. The Madagascar dry-spell gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation and have no normal-year comparison [ev_crop_yield_brue14_6]. The South African statement is a single commercial farmer's before-and-after testimony for a residue-cover system with no capture structure [ev_yield_stability_faocr11_10]. The Zambia review statement is cited secondhand, gives no magnitude and has no normal-year comparison, and the trial behind it bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zaï and tassa pits increase infiltration and the water retention capacity of the soil, so crops suffer less from drought spells at the onset of and during the rainy season [ev_soil_water_retention_kabo04_1, ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In rainfall-deficit periods zaï allowed cereals to be grown on degraded crusted soils in Burkina Faso, gave sorghum in a low-rainfall year where untreated land yielded nothing, and only tassa fields produced a harvest in the 1990 drought in Niger [ev_crop_yield_roose93_3, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_kabo04_6_s]. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers obtained 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 368 kg on conventional plots in the 2006/07 season, which the source calls a drought year [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In a Kenyan trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 2.53 against 1.82 t per hectare without inputs (not significant) and 4.10 against 3.15 t per hectare with manure and fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3]. Chololo pits in Tanzania are reported to mitigate drought effects [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_7]. Studies cited in a conservation agriculture meta-analysis report yields 10–100% higher than conventional tillage in relatively dry years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_6]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the contrast was 1520 against 400 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In on-farm conservation-farming trials in Kenya, Tanzania and Ethiopia the largest yield difference over conventional ploughing came in rainy seasons with low rainfall, when the practice maximises rainfall infiltration so the crop can bridge short periods of dry spell [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season of very scattered rainfall, maize in hand-hoe conservation-farming basins yielded 3,054 kg per hectare against 1,339 kg under ploughing, which the authors say showcased the water-harvesting benefits of the basins [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Zaï only reduces the impact of a dry spell of two to three weeks, and only where soil water storage capacity is at least 50 mm [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1]. In the Kenyan trial's short rains with meteorological droughts, tied ridging gave no advantage (0.52 against 0.53 t per hectare without inputs, 1.17 against 1.27 with manure and fertiliser) because there was little or no rainwater to hold in the basins [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_soil_water_retention_ndun23_1]. Conservation agriculture can reverse in extremes: in long-term Zimbabwe trials mulched and reduced-tillage maize yielded considerably less than conventional tillage in extreme seasons, and a study cited in the same meta-analysis reports yields 5–20% lower in wet years [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_4]. The zaï and tassa contrasts are author estimates, the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the Kenyan tied-ridging result comes from a single-site trial [ev_crop_yield_kabo04_1_s, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. Water harvesting is not irrigation, and the new primaries mark the limit: at the more arid Kenyan sites of Laikipia and Machakos each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, with 0 kg per hectare of maize harvested at Machakos due to meteorological drought, and the conservation-farming treatments did not avert it [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The East African low-rainfall gain is for the best system per site, ripping or pitting usually with fertiliser, so it is bundled with reduced tillage and fertiliser, and the authors read it as a trend from their own figure [ev_crop_yield_rock09_15]. The Zambia 2001/2 basin contrast is a raw comparison in a single season with no normal-year reference, and most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit, so part of the gap is the input package [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits concentrate runoff into the root zone, so crops can ride out a dry spell of two to three weeks. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: An expert statement from Burkina Faso, explicitly conditional on the soil having sufficient water storage capacity [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1], and an Ethiopian field observation of which plots wilted in dry spells, not a tested contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Infiltration trenches significantly reduced plot runoff across the reviewed mountain studies, a result the review files under runoff and flood reduction, and WOCAT compilers for tillage and pit systems in Niger, Kenya and Zambia rate downstream flooding as reduced [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1100_2011_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1219_2014_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1652_2014_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_940_2010_downstream_flooding, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1139_2013_downstream_flooding].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The trench result is plot-scale runoff rather than flood peaks or damage, and the remaining units are WOCAT compiler ratings, mostly slight [ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_1]. The Philippine sheet rates flood impacts as worse, and the Zambian compiler says the benefit holds only if applied on a large scale [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1021_2011_flood_impacts, ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1139_2013_downstream_flooding].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers for planting pits and stone lines, zai/tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger and conservation tillage in Kenya and Zambia judge downstream flooding reduced; the sheets describe no mechanism, and the Zambia compiler adds that the effect holds only if the practice is applied on a large scale.
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements, not measurements, mostly rated slight; the conservation-tillage sheet from the Philippines rated flood impacts worse, and conservation-tillage sheets are a loose fit for an in-situ water-harvesting family.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: A maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture performs better relative to conventional practice under drought and/or heat stress, the in-field mulch and reduced tillage carrying the effect [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This is a single meta-analytic statement for maize that does not separate heat from drought and gives no magnitude in the quoted passage, so the heat-specific effect is not isolated [ev_crop_yield_stew18_2].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture outperforms conventional practice at median rainfall and clay even without fertiliser and gains more as seasons get drier [ev_crop_yield_stew18_4, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; and earlier meta-analyses find no-till with residue retention and rotation raises rainfed yields by 7.3% in dry climates [ev_crop_yield_pittel15_2]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]; WOCAT compilers for pits, contour bunds and conservation tillage in several countries judge crop production increased. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated averaged 2.8 against 2.6 t per hectare on lowland and 2.4 against 2.1 on hillside fields, and year-to-year variability fell after consecutive years under the system (a 6% and a 13% decrease in the coefficient of variation) [ev_crop_yield_brue14_1, ev_crop_yield_brue14_2, ev_yield_stability_brue14_3, ev_yield_stability_brue14_4]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather give higher maize yields under conservation agriculture than under ploughing when aggregated across seasons, and more stable yields across different types of seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_5, ev_yield_stability_faocr11_6]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6], higher soil moisture improving yields in poor seasons [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3], and global syntheses: reduced tillage and crop residue management associated with a 106% increase in cereal yields, an average yield improvement of over 100% for smallholder conservation agriculture across 286 developing-country case studies, and a slight increase over conventional tillage, growing over time and especially in dry conditions, across 25 long-term trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect in a Kenyan season with a failed start, tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the system, and the pooled comparison showed no change in yield variance, the stability gain appearing only after consecutive years; the rice gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5, ev_yield_stability_brue14_7]. The crop-model results are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting; under sub-humid weather the model gives no difference [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_4], and in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both systems [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]; the 106% is for reduced tillage together with residue management [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13]; the poor-season result bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]; the over-100% figure comes from purposely selected best-practice projects [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15]; and the long-term trials are mainly from North America, Australia and Europe [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Zai pits, planting pits, contour bunds and reduced or ripper tillage raise and stabilise yields in dry years: compilers describe planting pits in Uganda keeping banana stands fruiting through drought and raising monthly harvests for sale, composting with planting pits in Burkina Faso raising farm income several times in dry years, and the Magoye ripper in Zambia improving yields and tolerance to dry spells at lower tillage cost [ev_food_security_wocat_1587_2013_risk_of_production_failure, ev_household_income_wocat_1587_2013_farm_income, ev_household_income_wocat_959_2010_farm_income, ev_household_income_wocat_1139_2013_farm_income]. In the literature, returns to labour for these practices in Burkina Faso exceed the shadow wage, and bunds show positive returns at subproject level in Mauritania [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1, ev_economic_return_mrt14_5]. Compilers also judge benefits to outweigh establishment and maintenance costs in both the short and the long term on every sheet that rates them. In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots in the low-rainfall budget, with 866.84 against 357.16 for experienced farmers in high rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2], and ground cover raised the odds of a Malawian plot meeting the household maize requirement in the El Niño season, and planting basins sharply raised those odds in a good Kenyan season [ev_food_security_boil19_1, ev_food_security_boil19_2]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the first-year margin was 473.36 against 48.19 US dollars per hectare [ev_economic_return_mazv09_3]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño season, no-till with a residue mulch returned a cost-benefit ratio of 1.39 against 1.05 for conventional tillage [ev_economic_return_mash25h1_3]. A review cites reduced tillage with residue maintained giving the highest net benefit and marginal rate of return on teff [ev_economic_return_tade23h1_4]. In Zambia, crop budgets for hand-hoe conservation-farming basins give returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional plowing for cotton, and returns to land and to peak-season labor 60 to 90 percent higher than hand hoe tillage for maize [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row now holds conflicting evidence. What pulls the in-field side apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages, and the practitioner ratings, put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution, and its revenue comes out ahead only when rainfall is far from the mean [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The other losses are season- or practice-specific: banking in Malawi's El Nino season, tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial [ev_food_security_boil19_3, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. Most units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT sheets, including the benefit-versus-cost judgements; the literature units are secondary model estimates for Burkina Faso and a lender self-reported subproject evaluation for Mauritania, and manual zai gives far smaller net benefits than mechanised zai in the same source [ev_economic_return_kabo04_1, ev_economic_return_mrt14_5, ev_economic_return_zoug14_1]. Several rated technologies bundle pits with compost or are conservation-tillage systems, and food security and farm income are proxies for poverty [ev_household_income_wocat_959_2010_farm_income, ev_food_security_wocat_1139_2013_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Cost savings from conservation agriculture are usually small for smallholders, and in a Kenyan drought season net benefits were higher without tied ridging except with Tithonia [ev_economic_return_corb20_1, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]; the Zimbabwe margins include manure and fertiliser with the high-rainfall figure a sensitivity scenario, and the Kenyan planting-basin odds ratio has a wide confidence interval [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2, ev_food_security_boil19_2]. In Malawi's El Nino season banking lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054, so a mis-timed in-field practice can cut food security rather than raise it [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. 30-cm zaï on the same Burkina Faso trial ran at a loss (−98 624 FCFA per hectare), smaller than the direct-seeding loss, and the investment counted is the experiment's own cost [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. The Zimbabwe ratio is a single drought-season budget with the mulch bundled with no-till [ev_economic_return_mash25h1_3]. The teff returns are cited second-hand [ev_economic_return_tade23h1_4]. The Zambian returns are crop budgets with output estimated from regression coefficients, bundled with early planting and purchased inputs (hybrid seed and fertiliser for maize), and the authors say early-planting gains dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. The Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue at later market prices with labour and non-market inputs unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: Infiltration trenches intercept and infiltrate runoff, cutting plot-level runoff and soil loss, with the runoff reduction larger on natural vegetation than on cropland [ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_1, ev_runoff_reduction_locat20_2]. WOCAT compilers rate zai and planting pits, contour bunds, basin tillage and conservation tillage as reducing soil loss and surface runoff, the Zambian ripper sheet attributing this to less soil disturbance and better soil cover [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_1139_2013_soil_loss, ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1139_2013_surface_runoff]. Meta-analyses now quantify the effect: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds soil loss cut by 68.67% under mulching and 54.97% under ridging and runoff by 57.2% and 53.6% [ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_2, ev_erosion_hazard_tefe24_3, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_2, ev_runoff_reduction_tefe24_4]; an Ethiopian synthesis reports soil loss down 59% under graded soil bunds, 88% under level soil bunds, 98% under mulch and 62% under tied ridging, with runoff down 25.2%, 60.1%, 75.5% and 55.8% [ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_1, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_2, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_4, ev_erosion_hazard_adim16_5, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_1, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_2, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_5, ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_4]; tied ridging in India reduced runoff by 69%, reviews report zai and tassa pits cutting runoff by 60–80% and high mulch cover by up to 79%, and Moroccan tabia store the runoff of all rains below 50 mm [ev_runoff_reduction_adim16_7, ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_1, ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_2, ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]. A meta-analysis of mulching finds runoff reduced by 47.4% and soil loss by 76.2% against controls, soil loss by 70.9% on cropland, and reductions of 45.9% and 75.1% at rainfall intensities above 90 mm/h [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_1, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_2, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_3, ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_5, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The literature units all come from a single review of trenches, largely in the Peruvian Andes (upper-middle income), which also reports increased catchment sediment in the first years after construction; plot-level effects may not transfer to catchments [ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_2, ev_erosion_hazard_locat20_3]. The rest are practitioner ratings, several for conservation-tillage systems, and the Zambian sheet expects reduced downstream siltation only if applied on a large scale [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1139_2013_downstream_siltation]. Tabia overflow and gully the slope in the biggest storms [ev_runoff_reduction_roos10_1]; the meta-analytic figures are unweighted means of plot studies and the pit and mulch ranges are review syntheses [ev_runoff_reduction_ngur26_1]. The mulching meta-analysis pools land uses including post-fire forest and bare land; cropland and tree crops were less effective in reducing runoff, both below 40%, and the mulching benefits decreased with increasing rainfall intensity under heavy rainfall [ev_runoff_reduction_fan23h1_4, ev_erosion_hazard_fan23h1_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices reduce what leaves the field. WOCAT compilers rate downstream siltation as reduced for zai and planting pits, planting pits with stone lines and contour bunds in Niger, and for conservation tillage in Zambia and Kenya [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1652_2014_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1219_2014_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1100_2011_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1139_2013_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_940_2010_downstream_siltation]. An Ethiopian synthesis finds graded soil bunds reduced the loss of soil organic matter by up to 52%, total nitrogen by up to 48% and available phosphorus by up to 41% [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: This row was previously split by a measured nitrogen increase under minimum tillage alone; that comparison has been removed because tillage alone, with no capture structure or soil cover, is not a water-harvesting practice, and the remaining evidence points one way. The gains are mostly for sediment, not nutrients: every siltation unit is a practitioner rating used as a component proxy, the Niger sheets for planting pits with stone lines and for contour bunds rate only a slight reduction, and the Zambian compiler expects the benefit only if the practice is applied on a large scale [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1100_2011_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1219_2014_downstream_siltation, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1139_2013_downstream_siltation]. The nutrient finding is a single synthesis for graded soil bunds [ev_nutrient_removal_adim16_1], so a project concerned with nutrient export downstream has one measured practice to go on. Nothing on water chemistry downstream is measured.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: WOCAT compilers judge contour bunds in Niger to improve water harvesting, and the compiler for ripper tillage in Zambia notes that the open furrows collect water [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1652_2014_harvesting_collection_of_water, ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1139_2013_harvesting_collection_of_water].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The WOCAT units are practitioner judgements rather than measurements, and the Zambian compiler says water availability improves only if the tillage is applied on a large scale [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_1139_2013_water_availability]. The Mauritanian well-level and Andean trench evidence now sits in the in-situ catchment water yield row, which also answers what upstream capture does to water downstream.

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In the humid Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where daily rains exceed 80 mm, zaï pits concentrate infiltration and sorghum in the pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields, and WOCAT compilers for pits and stone lines in Niger and conservation tillage in Kenya and the Philippines rate drainage of excess water as worse [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1100_2011_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_940_2010_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1021_2011_excess_water_drainage]. A conservation agriculture meta-analysis adds that 92% of the data show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering maize yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, waterlogging lasting 3–5 days during early maize growth also affected the mulching and basin treatments, whose waterlogged plants had yellow leaves and stunted growth [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. In a Kenyan on-farm trial, ridged plots with fertiliser at the relatively wetter sub-humid Rachuonyo site gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors and the rest are practitioner ratings, none quantified [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]. Compilers for ripper tillage in Zambia and composted planting pits in Burkina Faso rate drainage as improved, the Zambian one crediting better soil structure [ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1139_2013_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_959_2010_excess_water_drainage]. The meta-analysis figure is a share of observations, not an effect size [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]. The Ethiopian waterlogging finding is a field observation with no measured yield loss, and the source names a tillage treatment as the one particularly affected, so only part of the harm can be put on mulch and basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_1, ev_waterlogging_hazard_sime15h2_2]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. The Kenyan ridging loss is the authors' probable explanation rather than a measured waterlogging contrast, and the ridging is bundled with fertiliser; because it comes from using the practice at a wetter site than it suits, it is held out of the production classes as an envelope misfit (a suitability caveat) and counted here as waterlogging evidence [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6].

water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.mechanism: In-field practices hold water where the crop grows, which backfires in wet conditions: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rainfall exceeds 80 mm per day and 1 200 mm per year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than on flat-cultivated fields because of frequent soil waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; a conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds that 92% of the data show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]. WOCAT compilers for pits and stone lines in Niger and conservation tillage in Kenya and the Philippines rate drainage of excess water as worse [ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1100_2011_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_940_2010_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1021_2011_excess_water_drainage]. Primary sources from southern Africa make the same point: an FAO study shows by a water-balance calculation that planting basins can depress yields when too much water concentrates in them under high rainfall or in seasons with abnormally high rainfall, citing extension reports and farmer testimony of farmers scooping water from the basins [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8], and concludes that in sub-humid environments yields could be affected by water-logging in years with adequate rainfall [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7].
water_harvesting_conservation__water_har.conditionality: Compilers for ripper tillage in Zambia and composted planting pits in Burkina Faso rate drainage as improved, the Zambian one crediting improved soil structure [ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_1139_2013_excess_water_drainage, ev_waterlogging_hazard_wocat_959_2010_excess_water_drainage]. None of the harm sources gives a magnitude. The Cameroon zaï and mulch-cover losses come from using the practice outside its rainfall window; under the standing ruling they are held out of the production classes as performance caveats, and are counted here as waterlogging hazard evidence [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]. The Cameroon result is an unpublished observation cited by the authors, and the meta-analysis figure is a share of observations, not an effect size [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]. The southern African basin finding rests on a theoretical water balance plus extension reports and farmer testimony, and the author notes there are currently few published data to substantiate it [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_8]; the sub-humid conclusion goes beyond what the crop model simulates and covers conservation agriculture as basins or ripping with residue retention, so it is bundled with reduced tillage; neither gives a magnitude [ev_waterlogging_hazard_faocr11_7]. Most units carry no farming-system tag, so the rainfed reading rests largely on the practices being field-crop techniques.
